statement.given: Four personae: {name: 'stern', competence: true, friendliness: false}, {name: 'cool', competence: true, friendliness: true}, {name: 'asshole', competence: false, friendliness: false}, {name: 'doofus', competence: false, friendliness: true}. The prior over personae for a voter audience assigns probabilities [0.3, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2] to [stern, cool, asshole, doofus] respectively. Two morphological variants: 'n' and 'ng', both with production cost 0. Speaker optimality alpha = 6. Eckert-Montague semantics: 'ng' is consistent with a persona if that persona has competence = true or friendliness = false; 'n' is consistent with a persona if that persona has competence = false or friendliness = true.
statement.model: A literal listener for a variant samples from the voter persona prior, conditions on the variant being semantically consistent with the persona, and returns the persona. A speaker for a given persona draws uniformly from the two variants and weights each by alpha times (log-probability the literal listener assigns to that persona given the variant, minus the variant's cost). A naive pragmatic listener for a variant samples a persona from the voter prior and updates on the speaker choosing that variant.
statement.query: The posterior distribution over persona names for a naive pragmatic listener who hears the variant 'ng'.

statement.given: There are two restaurants, Burger Barn and Stirfry Shack. A group-level mean utility for each restaurant is drawn independently from a Beta(1,1) distribution (equivalent to a uniform distribution on [0,1]); a single group-level standard deviation, shared by both restaurants, is drawn from a uniform distribution on [0, 0.15]. Alice and three other agents each independently draw their own utility for each restaurant from a normal distribution centered at that restaurant's group-level mean with the group-level standard deviation; each individual utility draw is clipped to lie strictly between 0.001 and 0.999 (a draw at or below 0 becomes 0.001; a draw at or above 1 becomes 0.999). Alice chose Burger Barn and received a positive (successful) reward signal. The three other agents all chose Stirfry Shack (no reward signal is observed for any of them).
statement.model: Each agent's utility for a restaurant is that agent's believed probability that the restaurant gives a good experience. Alice's own reward signal for the restaurant she chose is a Bernoulli draw whose success probability is her own utility for that restaurant; her observed reward is soft evidence that this draw came out as observed. Each of the other three agents chooses a restaurant (between the two) with probability proportional to its own utility for that restaurant; each agent's own utility values are individually and independently drawn (as described above) and not directly observed by Alice, only its choice is. Their three observed choices are each soft evidence for this proportional-choice rule, under that agent's own latent utility values. Alice reasons jointly about the group-level mean utilities, the group-level standard deviation, her own utility for each restaurant, and the other three agents' utilities, conditioning on her own reward signal and the other three agents' observed choices.
statement.query: Report, as a two-field record, Alice's posterior distribution over her own utility for Burger Barn, and separately her posterior distribution over her own utility for Stirfry Shack, each estimated by sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with 10000 particles.

statement.given: There are three possible world states, equally likely a priori: no relevant individuals have the property ("No"), just some of them do ("Just some"), or all of them do ("All"). Six utterances are available, each equally likely under a base utterance prior before any reasoning about informativity: "some", "all", "no", "not all", "the", "not the". Their costs are: "the" 0, "not the" 1, "some" 1, "all" 1, "no" 1.5, "not all" 2. Four of the utterances have a fixed literal meaning, true in exactly these world states: "some" is true in Just some or All; "all" is true only in All; "no" is true only in No; "not all" is true in No or Just some. The meanings of "the" and "not the" are uncertain between two equally likely lexicons: under the first, "the" has the same truth conditions as "some" and "not the" has the same truth conditions as "no"; under the second, "the" has the same truth conditions as "all" and "not the" has the same truth conditions as "not all". A question under discussion is drawn (independently of the world state and the lexicon) from a distribution that places probability 0.8 on the question "what is the exact world state?", and probability 0.1 each on "is it the case that just some or all have the property?" and "is it the case that all have the property?". Each question partitions the three world states into equivalence classes: the first question distinguishes all three states from one another; the second groups {Just some, All} against {No}; the third groups {No, Just some} against {All}. The rationality parameter for all levels of pragmatic reasoning below is 5.
statement.model:
A literal listener, given an utterance and one of the two candidate lexicons, samples a world state uniformly and a question under discussion from the distribution above, discards any outcome where the utterance is not literally true of the sampled world under that lexicon, and reports the pair consisting of the equivalence class containing the (surviving) world under the sampled question, together with the question itself.

A level-1 speaker, for a given world state and question, computes an informativity score for each candidate utterance: the expectation, over the two lexicons (weighted by their 0.5/0.5 prior), of the log-probability the literal listener (under that lexicon) assigns to the pair (the true equivalence class of the world under the question, the question) when given that utterance, minus the utterance's cost. Utterances are otherwise drawn from the uniform base prior; the level-1 speaker reweights this prior by the exponential of the rationality parameter times the informativity score.

A level-n pragmatic listener (for n from 1 to 5), given an utterance, samples a world state uniformly and a question under discussion from the distribution above, and reweights this joint prior by the probability the level-n speaker assigns to the observed utterance given that world state and question.

For n from 2 to 5, a level-n speaker's informativity score for an utterance, given a world state and question, is the log-probability the level-(n-1) pragmatic listener assigns to that (world state, question) pair when given that utterance, minus the utterance's cost; the level-n speaker reweights the uniform base utterance prior by the exponential of the rationality parameter times this score, exactly as the level-1 speaker does with its own informativity score.
statement.query: For each of the six utterances ("some", "all", "no", "not all", "the", "not the"), report the level-5 pragmatic listener's posterior marginal distribution over the world state (No / Just some / All), after hearing that utterance.

statement.given:
There are four individuals. Each individual independently has an assignment of three boolean properties, called A, B, and C, drawn from a distribution over the eight possible combinations of (A, B, C). Two versions of this distribution are considered:

- Empirically-measured (the "lightbulb" domain): the eight combinations have the following probabilities, listed in the order (A,B,C) = (false,false,false), (false,false,true), (false,true,false), (false,true,true), (true,false,false), (true,false,true), (true,true,false), (true,true,true):
0.24602846414362, 0.11758230643016374, 0.03002454453076707, 0.021605845425660415, 0.09246959793518443, 0.11613603192957513, 0.1264134724274912, 0.24973973717753792.

- Idealized: each of the three properties is true independently of the others, each with probability 0.25, for every individual (so the eight combinations occur with probabilities determined by treating A, B, and C as three independent 0.25-coin flips).

Only situations in which each of the three properties A, B, and C is held by at least one of the four individuals are considered; other situations are excluded from consideration.

"Some X are Y" is true iff at least one individual has both X and Y. "None of the X are Y" is true iff no individual has both X and Y. "Not all X are Y" is true iff it is not the case that every individual with X also has Y.

A situation is drawn by independently assigning each of the four individuals a combination of the three properties, from the distribution in question (empirical or idealized). Conditioning on both stated premises being true of the drawn situation, consider the four possible conclusion sentences of the form "quantifier C are A", one for each of the four quantifiers (all, some, none, not all). Among the conclusion sentences that are true of the situation, one is drawn uniformly at random; that is the reported conclusion. Repeating this whole process (situation draw, conditioning on the premises, and uniform choice among the true conclusions) over and over defines a distribution over which conclusion sentence is reported.

statement.given:
Alice and Bob play a game of tug-of-war. Alice is strong with probability 0.5 (otherwise weak); independently, Bob is strong with probability 0.5 (otherwise weak). Independently of strength, Alice is lazy with probability 0.3 (otherwise not lazy); independently, Bob is lazy with probability 0.3 (otherwise not lazy). A strong player's pulling power is 2 and a weak player's is 1; a lazy player's pulling power is halved. Whichever player has the greater pulling power wins the game; if the two players' pulling powers are exactly equal, a fair coin (heads/tails each with probability 0.5) decides the winner. This whole process runs once to produce a single actual outcome: Alice's strength, Bob's strength, Alice's laziness, Bob's laziness, the tie-breaking coin (used only if needed), and the resulting winner.

Eighteen possible utterances describe this actual outcome:
- Two bare claims about the winner: "Alice won," "Bob won."
- Four bare claims about laziness: "Alice was lazy," "Bob was lazy," "Alice wasn't lazy," "Bob wasn't lazy."
- Four bare claims about strength: "Alice is strong," "Alice is weak," "Bob is strong," "Bob is weak."
- Eight paired claims, built from four (fact, outcome) pairs -- (Bob was lazy, Alice won), (Alice is strong, Alice won), (Alice wasn't lazy, Alice won), (Bob was weak, Alice won) -- each pair yielding both a plain-conjunction utterance ("[fact] and Alice won") and an explanatory utterance ("Alice won because [fact]").

Every bare utterance (ten of the eighteen) has cost 1; every paired utterance -- both plain-conjunction and explanatory (the remaining eight) -- has cost 6. An utterance's base prior probability, before any reasoning about truth or informativeness, is proportional to the exponential of the negative of its cost. The optimality/rationality parameter used at every reasoning level below is 5. The 'stickiness' parameter governing counterfactual similarity (described below) is 0.5.
statement.model:
A bare claim is true of the actual outcome exactly when its literal content holds there (e.g. "Alice won" is true iff Alice won; "Bob was lazy" is true iff Bob was lazy; "Alice wasn't lazy" is true iff Alice was not lazy). A plain-conjunction utterance "[fact] and Alice won" is true exactly when both the named fact and Alice's win hold in the actual outcome.

An explanatory utterance "Alice won because [fact]" is true of the actual outcome only through the following procedure. First, both the named fact and Alice's win must actually hold. Second, a further stochastic check must succeed: form a counterfactual outcome by taking the five independent random ingredients that generated the actual outcome (Alice's strength coin, Bob's strength coin, Alice's laziness coin, Bob's laziness coin, and the tie-breaking coin) and, independently for each one, either keep its actual value (with probability equal to the stickiness parameter) or redraw it fresh from its original probability (with the remaining probability); then run the same tug-of-war rules on these possibly-resampled ingredients to obtain the counterfactual outcome; restrict attention to instances of this construction where the named fact turns out false in the counterfactual outcome; the check succeeds exactly when, in such a restricted instance, Alice's win is also false there. The explanatory utterance's truth value is a single random draw of this whole two-part procedure -- so, granted that the fact and Alice's win both hold in the actual outcome, the explanatory utterance holds with probability equal to the chance that this counterfactual construction, conditioned on the named fact being false, also has Alice not winning.

A first listener, hearing one of the eighteen utterances, believes the actual outcome is drawn from the process above (independent strength, laziness, and any needed tie-break), conditioned on the heard utterance being true of it (using the truth procedure just described, including a fresh draw of the stochastic check for explanatory utterances).

A speaker, who knows the actual outcome, selects one of the eighteen utterances by starting from the cost-based utterance prior and reweighting each utterance's prior probability by the first listener's (for that utterance) probability of the actual outcome, raised to the power of the optimality parameter, then renormalizing.

A second listener, hearing only an utterance, infers the actual outcome by weighting each hypothesized outcome (drawn from the same base process) in proportion to the probability that a speaker who knew that outcome would have produced the heard utterance, that speaker probability itself raised to the power of the optimality parameter, then renormalizing.
statement.query: After hearing the utterance "Alice won because Bob was lazy," report the second listener's joint posterior probability distribution over the actual outcome: Alice's strength (strong or weak), Bob's strength (strong or weak), whether Alice was lazy, whether Bob was lazy, and the winner (Alice or Bob).

statement.given:
An event has a number of occurrences N and an average per-occurrence duration D, each ranging over the integers 1 through 10. For the topic of this problem — an ocean being cleaned — the three governing parameters are: alpha = 0.85, beta = 7, gamma = 20.

Define a discretized-Beta weighting function of two parameters g and d: it assigns to each of the ten integers 1 through 10 (via the ten evenly spaced points x = 0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0, where point x corresponds to integer round(10*x)) an unnormalized weight x^(g*d - 1) * (1-x)^((1-g)*d - 1); normalizing these ten weights gives a categorical distribution over 1 through 10.

The average duration D is drawn from this weighting function with g = alpha = 0.85 and d = beta = 7.
The number of occurrences N is drawn, independently of D, from a mixture: with probability 0.2, from the weighting function with g = 1 - alpha = 0.15 and d = beta = 7; with probability 0.8, from the weighting function with g = 0.1 and d = gamma = 20.

Two event-type readings are possible, "episodic" and "habitual," equally likely a priori.

An utterance describing the event names an object and, with probability 0.95, a specific timeframe drawn uniformly at random from the integers 1 through 10; with probability 0.05, the utterance instead carries no timeframe (a bare, uninformative form).

Speaker cost: an utterance with an explicit timeframe costs 1; the no-timeframe utterance costs 2. The speaker-optimality parameter is 1.

The observed utterance names the object "ocean" together with the timeframe 10.
statement.model:
An utterance with an explicit timeframe T is true of a given (N, D, event-type reading) exactly when the total elapsed duration N*D is at least T, and additionally: under the episodic reading, N must equal 1; under the habitual reading, N must be greater than 1. The no-timeframe utterance is true regardless of N, D, or the reading.

A literal listener, given an utterance (naming an object and, possibly, a timeframe) and an event-type reading, infers (N, D) by conditioning the object's (N, D) prior described above on the utterance being true of (N, D) under that reading.

A speaker, who knows the object, the true event-type reading, and the true (N, D), chooses an utterance (naming the same object, with a timeframe or the no-timeframe form as described above) with probability proportional to the literal listener's probability of assigning the true (N, D) to that utterance and reading, raised to the speaker-optimality power, discounted by the utterance's cost (a fixed cost is subtracted before exponentiating, not scaled by the optimality parameter).

A pragmatic listener, upon hearing an utterance for a given object, jointly infers the event-type reading (uniform prior) and (N, D) (drawn from the object's prior), reweighting in favor of reading/(N, D) combinations under which the speaker described above would have been likely to produce exactly the observed utterance.
statement.query: Given the utterance naming "ocean" with timeframe 10, report the pragmatic listener's posterior as three separate marginal distributions: over the number of occurrences N (an integer from 1 to 10); over the average per-occurrence duration D (an integer from 1 to 10); and over the event-type reading (episodic vs. habitual).

statement.given: Fifteen marbles are thrown into a pond; each independently either sinks or floats. The world is one of two regimes, equally likely a priori (probability 0.5 each): a normal world in which each marble sinks with probability 0.99, and a wonky world in which each marble sinks with probability 0.5. The world state is the number of marbles that sink (an integer from 0 to 15). Three utterances are available, each equally likely a priori: "Some", "All", "None". Their literal meanings: "Some" is true when at least one marble sinks; "All" is true when all fifteen sink; "None" is true when none sink. The speaker-optimality parameter is 1. The observed utterance is "Some".
statement.model: A Rational Speech Act model. A literal listener hears an utterance and infers the world state, conditioning on the utterance being literally true given the world's per-marble sinking probability. A speaker who knows the world state chooses an utterance with probability proportional to the literal listener's probability of that true world state, with the utility scaled by the speaker-optimality parameter. The pragmatic listener hears the speaker's utterance and jointly infers whether the world is wonky and the world state (the number of marbles that sink); it also draws a fresh next-world state from the same inferred regime.
statement.query: After hearing the speaker say "Some", report the pragmatic listener's posterior as three marginal distributions: the number of marbles that sink (integer 0 to 15); whether the world is wonky (a boolean); and the next-world number of marbles that sink (integer 0 to 15).
